sections.text: Max Verstappen won the Las Vegas Grand Prix after a race defined by 34 lead changes. The event involved constant battling between Red Bull, Mercedes, and McLaren. George Russell crashed late in the race, while Kimi Antonelli lost positions to Lando Norris and Oscar Piastri on the final lap. Ferrari drivers Charles Leclerc and Lewis Hamilton both received 10-second penalties for driving infringements.

sections.text: The race was described as reminiscent of American oval racing, differing significantly from typical Formula 1 events. It highlighted the impact of the Las Vegas circuit and energy-starved hybrid engines on competitive dynamics. The high number of overtakes and the unpredictable nature of the lead battles provided significant entertainment value.

gist: COP31 in Antalya collapsed after failing to reach consensus on mentioning fossil fuels.
Countries split over whether an agreement without explicit fossil fuel phase-out language was acceptable.
The deadlock has intensified calls to reform the UN climate summit process.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The COP31 climate summit in Antalya, Turkey, collapsed without a final overarching agreement after negotiations hit unbridgeable red lines over fossil fuels. A proposed compromise text failed to mention fossil fuels directly, prompting roughly two-thirds of attending countries, including EU member states, to reject it. Oil-producing nations opposed explicit phase-out language and climate finance terms, leading to the longest UN climate summit ending in deadlock.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The breakdown highlights deep geopolitical divisions and raises questions about the effectiveness of the consensus-based COP model. Critics and officials argued that allowing a small group of petrostates veto power over vital climate action undermines global progress. However, supporters noted that despite the summit's failure, renewable energy transitions continue to advance in the real world.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: UN climate chief Simon Stiell acknowledged the need to reform the COP process, with some governments proposing the introduction of voting or the creation of voluntary agreements outside formal talks for countries wanting to move faster.

gist: A third of young British adults have never had sex, according to a major study.
Adults in Great Britain are having sex less frequently than in past decades.
Online sexual activities like sexting and watching pornography have become widespread among young people.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The fourth National Survey of Sexual Attitudes and Lifestyles found British adults are having less sex. Under-45s average sex twice a month, down from four times in 1990. A third of under-25s have never had sex, up from under a fifth in 2010. Meanwhile, half of 16- to 24-year-olds have sent or received sexual images in the past year.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Fewer young women want children, with the proportion doubling to 17% over the past decade. Researchers cite potential factors like economic insecurity, mental health issues, less physical socialising, and living with parents longer. Furthermore, many people still engage in unprotected sex, putting them at risk of sexually transmitted infections and unplanned pregnancies.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Researchers plan to investigate what is driving changing family plans and potential future impacts of AI companions on sexual behaviour. Public health services may also need to adapt to ensure equitable HPV vaccination coverage across all groups.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Metropolitan Police officers seized 893kg of suspected cocaine and £450,000 in cash during an operation targeting organised crime groups. gist: The US Army plans to detonate unstable lead azide in Middletown, Iowa.
The explosion was delayed several times due to legal challenges and public concern.
Local residents and farmers are taking precautions against potential toxic lead dust.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The US Army scheduled a controlled explosion of 68 barrels of unstable lead azide at an ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. The detonation followed several delays caused by public outcry, legal actions from environmental groups, and intervention by Donald Trump. Outlets reported the scheduled time as 10:00 EST and 9:00 CST.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Lead azide is an explosive compound that has crystallised and degraded over decades, creating a risk of spontaneous detonation. A controlled blast aims to limit toxic lead dust, which could travel up to 100 miles and potentially affect hundreds of nearby farms, local communities and water supplies.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Officials recommend that residents within five miles evacuate, while those within 20 miles should stay indoors. The military is using water walls, foam, and gel blocks to contain dust. Further environmental and health testing has been urged.

gist: Franz Josef village faces severe flood risks as its local riverbed rises rapidly.
Scientists urge urgent action to release river waters and prevent a potential disaster.
Local authorities and the community are discussing costly relocation and mitigation strategies.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A technical report released in September revealed that the Waiho River is rising and changing course much faster than previously predicted, putting the tourist village of Franz Josef at risk of catastrophic flooding.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The rising riverbed, trapped by stopbanks, sits above the adjacent land. Without urgent intervention, the village faces severe damage or destruction, alongside earthquake risks and potential loss of life.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: A working group aims to present a management plan to the government in early 2027. A future government will then decide how to address the situation.

gist: The UK sanctioned top Myanmar military leaders following an ICJ genocide ruling.
The ICJ ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya minority.
Malaysia announced plans to deport thousands of Myanmar refugees despite UN warnings.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The International Court of Justice ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Rohingya minority. Following the judgment, the UK sanctioned five senior Myanmar military leaders and announced legislation to block aviation fuel exports. Meanwhile, Malaysia announced it would deport thousands of Myanmar migrants and refugees back to their home country.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: This ruling marks the first time the court has found a state responsible for genocide. The 2017 military campaign forced over 700,000 Rohingya to flee to Bangladesh. Although Malaysia stated that hosting refugees has created financial and security burdens, the UN warned against returning people to dangerous conditions in Myanmar.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The UK will raise the ruling at the UN Security Council and host a dedicated meeting. In December, Malaysia plans to return 1,500 people by naval ships, with thousands more scheduled to be flown back.

sections.text: In March, the UK Home Office introduced an emergency visa brake on study visas for applicants from Afghanistan, Cameroon, Myanmar and Sudan. Consequently, Afghan women holding UK university offers had their visa applications halted.

sections.text: Women in Afghanistan face severe restrictions under the Taliban, including bans on secondary and higher education. Applicants overcame significant hurdles to secure UK places, but the UK government cited high asylum claim rates for pausing visas.

gist: The inaugural Children's Booker prize has announced its eight-book shortlist.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The Booker Prize Foundation has revealed the shortlist for its first children's fiction award. The list, known as the Great Eight, was selected from 89 submissions by a panel including author Frank Cottrell-Boyce, actor Lolly Adefope, and bookseller Sanchita Basu De Sarkar. Four child judges, selected from thousands of applicants, will join the panel to determine the winner. The prize offers £50,000, matching the award for adult fiction.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The prize was established amid concerns regarding declining rates of reading enjoyment among children. Organisers aim to bring children's books into the limelight and address the lack of prestige often afforded to the genre. By providing 30,000 copies of the shortlisted books to children in need, the foundation hopes to encourage reading and foster a broader cultural conversation about its importance.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The winning book will be announced on 2 February at the Young V&A in London. Leading up to the ceremony, a series of short films featuring various performers reading extracts from the shortlisted titles will be released.

sections.text: Over 160 writers signed an open letter warning that draft proposals for Northern Ireland's public libraries could lead to book bans, restrictions on minority group visibility, and library closures. Communities Minister Gordon Lyons stated that librarians will decide which books to stock while policy will keep flags, emblems, and political displays off premises.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Authors including Claire Allan, Stephen Daly, and Brian McGilloway warned that neutral space proposals amount to stealth censorship, risking the visibility of marginalised groups such as LGBTQ people and people of colour. Conversely, Gordon Lyons argued libraries should remain open to everyone on the same basis, free from political displays.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The Department for Communities consultation regarding the draft policy for library services closes at 23:59 GMT on Wednesday.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Excerpts from the private diary of the late Pope Francis have been published. The entries, written between 1992 and 2024, reveal the pontiff claimed to have seen the devil three times. He described the devil as having a raspy voice and menacing, flaming eyes. The diary also documents his internal reflections on his papacy, including a period of spiritual crisis and his self-criticism regarding personal pride and anger. Additionally, the book includes his thoughts on various church officials.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The diary provides insight into the personal struggles and spiritual experiences of the late leader of the Catholic Church. It specifically highlights his deep regret over his 2018 visit to Chile, where he initially defended a bishop accused of covering up sexual abuse. Francis admitted he failed to grasp the severity of the situation at the time, later describing the scandal as a vision of the gates of hell.

gist: England recorded an estimated 5,258 heat-linked deaths during the hottest summer on record.
The UK Health Security Agency reported seven heat episodes lasting 41 days in 2026.
Officials and experts are calling for urgent long-term adaptation to extreme heat risks.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: England experienced its hottest summer on record in 2026, resulting in an estimated 5,258 heat-associated deaths. This figure is the highest since records began in 2016 and nearly doubles the previous record of 2,985 deaths in 2022. The UK Health Security Agency identified seven distinct heat episodes between May and August, totalling 41 days. The deadliest period occurred in late June, coinciding with temperatures reaching 38C.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Experts warn that climate change is increasing the frequency and intensity of extreme heat, creating a growing public health emergency. The UK Health Security Agency emphasised that early summer heat can be particularly dangerous as public services may be unprepared. Health Secretary Yvette Cooper stated that the NHS must now prepare for summer with the same seriousness as winter.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The government is under pressure to improve long-term adaptation, including heat-proofing homes, schools, and care settings. Officials are prioritising systemic preparation to mitigate future health impacts as extreme weather events are expected to become more common.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Tidal announced a full ban on music generated entirely by AI. The company plans to delete 27 to 29 million tracks from its platform beginning December 9. This decision follows a significant increase in AI-generated uploads, which accounted for 43 percent of new submissions over the past 90 days.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Tidal stated that AI-generated content harms human artists by siphoning royalty payments and burying authentic music. While other major platforms like Spotify and YouTube Music primarily label AI content, Tidal is taking a stricter approach to maintain the quality of its catalog. Most of the tracks slated for removal have received no streams.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Tidal will begin rejecting daily submissions that are fully AI-generated and will prevent distribution services from delivering such content. The platform will continue to accept music that uses AI tools provided the final product includes human elements.

fivew: Tidal is banning and deleting all music tracks generated entirely by AI.
The removal process begins on December 9, 2026.
The policy applies to the Tidal music streaming platform.
To prevent AI content from harming human artists and burying authentic music.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Reform UK members attempted to remove the Senedd's Presiding Officer, Huw Irranca-Davies, following a dispute over the suspension of member Joe Martin. The motion was defeated by 55 votes to 29. Reform UK had previously boycotted most Senedd proceedings after Martin was asked to apologise for comments regarding immigration.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The dispute highlights tensions over parliamentary standards and free speech. Reform UK claims the Presiding Officer silenced an elected member and negotiated in bad faith. Conversely, the Llywydd maintains he must apply rules impartially to prevent intimidation and ensure standards in the chamber.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Reform UK has stated it will escalate the situation following the failed vote. The Llywydd's office maintains that his position on the requirement for an apology has remained consistent throughout the process.

articles.standfirst: A new AI-assisted proof seems to be solid, but we're not sure what it tells us.

timeline.text: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?

gist: A mathematician used AI to help produce a proof of the Riemann hypothesis.
The proof is currently being verified by the mathematics community.
AI usage in mathematics raises concerns about the loss of human insight.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Levent Alpöge, a mathematician working at Anthropic, announced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis using the AI model Claude. The proof exists in two forms: a rigorous description in the programming language Lean for verification and a description of the underlying logic.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The Riemann hypothesis is a significant problem in mathematics with implications for number theory and cryptography. While AI can efficiently generate proofs, mathematicians worry that the opaque reasoning of neural networks may deprive the field of the valuable insights and new tools typically gained through the human process of discovery.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Mathematicians are currently reviewing the proof. It remains unclear whether the AI-generated logic will provide the field with new mathematical understanding or if it will take years for humans to extract meaningful insights from the work.

fivew: A mathematician announced a proof of the Riemann hypothesis using AI.

sections.text: Sales of motorised quadricycles, or micro-cars, have increased significantly across Europe over the last five years. These vehicles, which do not require a standard driving licence, are increasingly popular with teenagers and older people in rural areas. The launch of the electric Citroën Ami in 2020 helped shift the market, attracting younger buyers who previously used mopeds or scooters. Manufacturers have responded to this demand by expanding production and developing more sophisticated models.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: These cars provide essential mobility for those without a full licence, including young people and those living in areas with limited public transport. While they offer independence, they are restricted to lower speeds and are forbidden on motorways. Some users express concerns regarding safety when sharing roads with faster traffic, describing the vehicles as vulnerable compared to larger cars and trucks.

sections.text: Leaked data from the Russian statistics agency Rosstat, analysed by the BBC, suggests that 490,334 Russian soldiers have died since the invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. sections.text: The figures highlight the severe human cost of the conflict, particularly for young Russian men. In 2025, the war accounted for 65% of deaths among Russian men aged 18 to 24. sections.text: A study from University College London analysed data from nearly 8,000 women in England. It found that women aged 45-60 are the least likely group to successfully quit smoking. Only 18% of this demographic succeeded, compared to higher rates in younger and older women.

gist: Hundreds complained about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu aggressive.
Frostrup discussed gender double standards, whilst Odudu highlighted how language affects Black women.
ITV stated it monitors camp contestants constantly and takes duty of care seriously.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Hundreds of people complained about I'm A Celebrity after Mariella Frostrup called AJ Odudu aggressive. Frostrup argued that forthright women are often labelled aggressive, whereas forthright men are called strong. Odudu agreed with the point on gender but explained that the word carries extra weight when used in casual scenarios towards Black women. Friction resurfaced when Frostrup remarked that Odudu did not take an apology well.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The exchange highlighted sensitive conversations around race and gender-based language on television. ITV stated that production monitors camp members constantly, maintaining measures to protect contestant welfare and intervening if anyone uses inappropriate language or oversteps the line.

quotes.text: Well, I wasn't being aggressive, so it shouldn't have been there.
you don't take an apology well

gist: A three-year-old boy died after choking on food at a Greater Manchester nursery.
Greater Manchester Police are investigating the death, and no arrests have been made.
Regulator Ofsted suspended Cosy Toes nursery for six weeks following the incident.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Thiago Wall, aged three, suffered an unsurvivable brain injury after choking on food at Cosy Toes nursery in Middleton on 2 November. He was taken to hospital and died three days later.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Regulator Ofsted suspended Cosy Toes Nursery Ltd from operating its four Middleton nurseries for six weeks due to child safety concerns. Greater Manchester Police are investigating the tragedy.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: The police investigation will take months rather than weeks. Ofsted may extend the nursery suspension, and no date has been set for a full inquest.

gist: Approaching storms and strong winds threaten Thanksgiving travel and parade plans in New York.
High wind gusts could force organisers to ground the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade balloons.
Heavy rain, flooding, power outages and flight delays are expected along the US east coast.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: A severe storm system moving up the US east coast brings heavy rain and strong wind warnings. The storm threatens to disrupt Thanksgiving travel and events, including the Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade in New York City.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: New York City guidelines ban parade inflatables if sustained winds exceed 23mph or gusts surpass 34mph. High winds could ground the balloons or force organisers to start the parade earlier. Heavy rain, coastal flooding, power outages and flight delays may also disrupt holiday travel for millions of Americans.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Winds are forecast to strengthen through Thursday, peaking in the evening. The storm will move over Cleveland, Buffalo and New England, with wintry weather and rain spreading across eastern areas through Friday.

gist: US stock market indices fell as shares in major technology firms connected to AI dropped.
Investors worry about AI investment sustainability, Democrat election gains, and leadership turmoil at Nvidia.
The US government announced new tariffs as part of President Donald Trump's trade policy.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: US stock market indices fell on Wednesday, with the Nasdaq dropping almost 4%. Shares in major technology companies including Nvidia, Anthropic, Amazon, Tesla and SpaceX, Micrsoft and Meta all declined. The US government also announced new tariffs under President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Investors are concerned about the sustainability of massive AI investments. Market volatility has also been driven by Democrat gains in the US midterm elections and turmoil surrounding Nvidia boss Jensen Huang following his temporary resignation.

sections.heading: What happens next
sections.text: Democrat politicians have campaigned for tougher AI regulation and a data centre moratorium. Investment bank Goldman Sachs expects AI investment to exceed $1 trillion in 2026.

gist: The inaugural Children's Booker prize announced its shortlist and child judges.
Child judges will help decide the winner alongside adult judges on the panel.
The winning book will be announced in February next year in London.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: The first Children's Booker prize revealed its shortlist and the children chosen to judge the books. A panel of child judges, along with adults including Frank Cottrell-Boyce, Lolly Adefope and Sanchita Basu De Sarkar, will determine the winner. The announcement of the victorious book is scheduled for February next year at the Young V and A in London, accompanied by the distribution of 30,000 copies to children in need.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The prize aims to address concerning statistics regarding declining reading enjoyment among children and young people. By including children on the judging panel, the organisers ensure that young readers have a direct and powerful voice in deciding which book deserves to win.

gist: Sabrina Bahsoon experienced sudden psychotic symptoms initially misdiagnosed as stress and lack of sleep.
She was sectioned before doctors discovered she had anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis caused by ovarian tumours.
Bahsoon is now recovering in Malaysia and hopes to raise awareness of the rare disease.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Content creator Sabrina Bahsoon began experiencing erratic behaviour and psychotic symptoms in March. After being discharged from A&E with sleeping tablets, police brought her to hospital where she was sectioned and treated with antipsychotic medication. Two months later, she was diagnosed with anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis caused by ovarian tumours, and had surgery in June.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: Bahsoon wants to raise awareness of the rare autoimmune disease and encourage people to advocate for their treatment. An NHS trust apologised after an internal review found initial assessment aspects were not followed up properly.

fivew: Sabrina Bahsoon was misdiagnosed with psychosis before discovering she had anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis.
To raise awareness of the rare disease and encourage people to advocate for themselves.

sections.heading: What happened
sections.text: Mauricio Pochettino began his tenure as Manchester United manager with a 4-0 defeat at Liverpool. Leny Yoro was shown a red card after eight minutes, and United quickly conceded two goals.

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.text: The heavy defeat leaves United 19th in the Premier League table after 11 games, highlighting the massive scale of the task facing Pochettino after leaving his United States job.
